doc.title: Bobby Johnson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, Ellenville, New York, June 23, 1998

title: Recording Tippin' In with the Harmon mute
summary: The Chicago RCA session where he dropped his cup mute, used a Harmon mute and made the hit solo.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Growl, plunger and derby: the trumpet mute tradition

blocks.x: Can you tell me about that recording session that you did “Tippin’ In?”
The recording session where you did “Tippin’ In” with the mute?

Well how this came about, we had rehearsed “Tippin In” it was written by Bobby Smith. We had rehearsed it in Boston. And at that particular time the union was on strike. [Scats] which had like a wartime flavor. So we were supposed to come to New York but they told us instead of coming to New York, since we was already out west, to go to RCA Victor out by the stockyards in Chicago. So about five below zero I think that morning, we went and we’d all been drinking that night for some reason, I don’t know why, we’d all been drinking that night. So we said well let’s try that “Tippin’ In.” And we played it first and we went down, and during those days it was before tape. It was on the disks. The more we played it, the worse we got. So one of the A&R men I think was Russ Case, a fine trumpet player, he was RCA Victor’s A&R man. He said let’s go back and try the first one. So while I was going to the mic, I dropped my cup mute and he threw me, what we call — I can’t think of them—
That’s it. You know better than I do. A Harmon mute. And when it got to my solo the guys said, down low, and a million, I’d say two million records came from that, and twenty-one dollars for me.
So you could buy your own Harmon mute, right?

Yeah. I could buy my own Harmon. Now the story is that is where the Miles Davis sound came from. It doesn’t have to be true. I’d like for it maybe to be true because Miles, as you know Miles took my place with the Benny Carter band.
